answer: Fluorescence is unlikely to report glucose, because the sources list fluorophores such as NADH, tryptophan and riboflavin and assign glucose to NIR and Raman. NIR is the method to test first for glucose and, combined with fluorescence, may improve biomass, but viable biomass needs an independent viability reference that the sources do not provide.

problems.text: Fluorimetry is highly sensitive but has low selectivity and relies on secondary emission from substances that are mostly biological; most chemicals do not fluoresce, so sensitivity alone does not make it a glucose method.
There is no direct fluorescence route to glucose: the listed intrinsic fluorophores are NADH, tryptophan and riboflavin, while glucose is assigned to NIR and Raman.
High sensitivity suits trace cofactors, not glucose: NIR tracks major components such as glucose in the millimolar range, while fluorescence works at nM to µM for trace fluorophores.

Viable biomass has no defined signal or reference: turbidity correlates with cell density, and NIR combined with fluorescence improved biomass estimates in yeast, but no viable-cell measurement is described, so an independent viability reference must be defined first.

methods.why: Tracks glucose in the millimolar range and is the most common online fiber-probe method; it needs chemometric models.
Gives direct detection of glucose in aqueous media; signals are weak and can be masked by fluorescence of some compounds.
A low-cost turbidity signal that correlates with cell density, but its selectivity is low.
Detects NADH, tryptophan and riboflavin at high sensitivity; useful for biomass only in combination with NIR, not for glucose.

questions.q: Is the broth transparent or opaque during the run, and what glucose range do you expect?
questions.why: Opacity decides the probe type, and the glucose range decides whether NIR's sensitivity is enough.

questions.q: What exactly is viable biomass for you, and which independent laboratory method will provide the reference?
questions.why: No viable-cell measurement appears in the sources, so a biomass model would have no reference.

questions.q: Does the broth contain any fluorescent component, such as NADH, tryptophan or riboflavin, that you can measure?
questions.why: Fluorescence is limited to samples with at least one fluorescent component, so this decides whether it can add anything.

questions.q: What accuracy, measurement range and response time do you need for glucose and biomass?
questions.why: Without these targets no go or no-go criteria can be set.

experiment.objective: Test whether NIR, with Raman as comparator, predicts glucose and viable biomass in the fermenter against independent laboratory reference values.
steps: Record NIR spectra with the probe in the fermenter across several batches, and take samples at the same times.
Measure glucose and viable biomass on the same samples with independent laboratory analyses, not the instrument's own calibration.
Build PLS chemometric models per method and validate them on held-out batches.
Record Raman spectra on the same samples and compare them with NIR on the same validation data.
If fluorescence is added for biomass, accept a combined NIR + fluorescence model only if it beats NIR alone on the same validation data.
references: S01 p.16 (glucose by NIR and Raman; biomass by turbidity)
S01 p.5 (chemometric models built, validated, then applied)

multispectral.why: NIR tracks the major component glucose, while fluorescence detects trace fluorophores at high sensitivity; the yeast fermentation example improved biomass with this pair.
multispectral.test: On the same validation batches, compare NIR alone with NIR + fluorescence for viable biomass; accept the combination only if it beats NIR alone.
